description: We are PyCoders, a student team from IUBAT in Dhaka, Bangladesh, working on the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge. Our project, FloodCast Radar, uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data to detect and map monsoon floods through cloud cover. It tracks new flooding across all 64 districts of Bangladesh every 12 days on a simple interactive map for disaster managers, NGOs and communities.
summary: FloodCast Radar is a web application that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into a clear, district-by-district flood map of Bangladesh. During the monsoon, clouds hide the ground from optical satellites exactly when floods happen, but NISAR's L-band radar sees through clouds, day and night. Our pipeline detects new water in each radar image, removes permanent rivers, and measures the flooded area in all 64 districts every 12-day cycle. Disaster managers, NGOs, local officials and families can see where the water is, whether it is rising or falling, and where help is needed first.
details:
THE CHALLENGE WE ANSWER

"Dancing with the SARs" asks for an interactive application that uses NISAR radar data to track and visualize surface change. We chose the change that affects millions of people in our country every year: monsoon flooding in Bangladesh. When rivers like the Jamuna rise, families and relief teams all ask the same question: where is the water right now, and where is it going? Optical satellites cannot answer during the monsoon because of clouds. Radar can, but its data comes as huge, technical files that responders cannot use directly. FloodCast Radar closes that gap.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find: our Python pipeline searches NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) DAAC for every NISAR L2 GCOV image over Bangladesh, starting from 17 June 2026, so the whole 2026 monsoon is covered.

2. Detect water: smooth water reflects the radar signal away, so it appears dark. We average pixels to reduce speckle, convert backscatter to decibels and use an automatic Otsu threshold. If an image has too little water/land contrast, it borrows a trusted threshold so it does not report false floods.

3. Remove normal water: pixels that are water in at least 90% of images (rivers, beels, permanent radar shadow) are treated as normal water, not flood.

4. Measure districts: new water is counted inside the official boundaries of all 64 districts and grouped into NISAR's 12-day cycles, giving flooded km², % flooded and observation coverage for every district.

5. Show and alert: a Django backend stores the results and serves an API to a Leaflet + Chart.js dashboard with a colour-coded district map, a date slider with a Play button to watch the monsoon spread and recede, a national timeline, a top-10 list of worst-hit districts, district detail pages and flood alerts. A daily scheduler checks for new images, so the site updates itself automatically (near real-time, limited by NISAR's ~12-day revisit).

WHY IT MATTERS

Disaster managers and NGOs see where to send help first, local officials see whether water is rising or falling, journalists and researchers get open data and a clear method, and families can check their own district. Everything works at district level, the unit that governments and relief agencies actually use.

HONESTY AND VALIDATION

We tested our flood-detection method on simulated radar data: a planted flood of 2,827 km² was measured as 2,815 km² (99.6%). Testing also revealed a false-flood bug in low-water images, which we fixed. NISAR data is still provisional, so the app labels it clearly and shows coverage for every district. Known limits: radar shadow in hill districts, floodwater under dense crops, and the 12-day revisit.

DATA AND TOOLS

NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV data (provisional) via NASA ASF DAAC, which brings in data from both NASA and ISRO; district boundaries from geoBoundaries (CC BY 4.0). Built with Python, Google Colab, asf_search, h5py, NumPy, scikit-image, rasterio, GeoPandas, Django, SQLite, Leaflet, Chart.js and Bootstrap.

WHAT WE WOULD BUILD NEXT

Estimate the number of people affected by combining flood maps with open population data; measure farmland under water; add a terrain mask for hill districts; detect flooded vegetation using L-band double-bounce signals; send Bangla flood alerts to union-level officials; track river-bank erosion on the Jamuna and Padma; and extend coverage to other flood-prone countries in South Asia.
